# Lint rules

<!-- Generated by `medaka lint --list-rules --markdown`. Do not edit by hand. -->

Every rule `medaka lint` knows. `universal` rules are meaningful in any Medaka program; `internal` rules enforce this repository's own conventions. `gated` rules must have zero findings across the enforced tree; `baselined` rules may only fall (`docs/ops/CLI-CONFORMANCE.md`, `.githooks/pre-commit`). Per-rule detail: `medaka lint --explain <rule>`.

## rule-match-on-param

function body is a `match` on a bare parameter (prefer multi-clause; STYLE §8)

A function whose whole body is a `match` on one of its own parameters is clearer as several clauses: the patterns move into the parameter position and the extra indentation level goes away. This enforces STYLE section 8, a repository taste ruling.

```
Before:
  len xs = match xs
    [] => 0
    _ :: t => 1 + len t
After:
  len [] = 0
  len (_ :: t) = 1 + len t
```

## rule-hand-rolled-derivable

hand-written Eq/Ord/Debug impl that could be `deriving` (STYLE §6)

A hand-written `Eq`, `Ord` or `Debug` impl that does exactly what `deriving` would generate is code that can drift from the type. Derive it instead.

```
Before:
  impl Eq Color
    Red == Red = True
    ...
After:
  data Color = Red | Green deriving (Eq)
```

## rule-stdlib-reimpl

top-level function reimplements a stdlib function under a different name (same declared signature) (STYLE §7a)

A top-level function whose declared signature equals that of an exported stdlib function, and whose body does the same work, reimplements the stdlib under another name. The rule compares against the stdlib signature index. Call the stdlib function.

```
Before:
  sumAll : List Int -> Int
  sumAll xs = foldl (+) 0 xs
After:
  use `sum` from the stdlib
```

## rule-bind-then-destructure

do-bind then immediately destructures the bound var with an irrefutable single-arm `match`. Inline the pattern into the bind

A `do` bind that immediately destructures the bound variable with an irrefutable single-arm `match` can put the pattern in the bind itself.

```
Before:
  p <- getPair
  match p
    (a, b) => use a b
After:
  (a, b) <- getPair
  use a b
```

## rule-lambda-section

lambda whose body is a single binary op on its parameter(s). Prefer an operator section (STYLE "Dogfooding")

A lambda whose body is a single binary operator applied to its parameter is an operator section. The section is shorter and names no throwaway variable.

```
Before:
  map (x => x + 1) xs
After:
  map (+ 1) xs
```

## rule-if-max-min

if-then-else selects the larger/smaller of the same two operands. Prefer `max`/`min`

An `if` that picks the larger or smaller of two operands is `max` or `min`.

```
Before:
  if a > b then a else b
After:
  max a b
```

## rule-andthen-pure-map

monadic bind whose continuation just wraps a pure transformation (`andThen m (x => pure body)`). Prefer `map` (functor law: m >>= (pure . f) ≡ fmap f m)

A monadic bind whose continuation only wraps a pure transformation in `pure` is `map`, by the functor law `m >>= (pure . f) == fmap f m`.

```
Before:
  andThen m (x => pure (f x))
After:
  map f m
```

## rule-destructure-in-param

function body is a single-arm `match` on a bare parameter with an irrefutable pattern (tuple/record/single-ctor). Destructure directly in the parameter position

A function body that is a single-arm `match` on a bare parameter with an irrefutable pattern (tuple, record, single-constructor) can destructure in the parameter position.

```
Before:
  f p = match p
    (a, b) => a + b
After:
  f (a, b) = a + b
```

## rule-missing-signature

top-level value/function binding has no sibling type signature (name : Type). Add one (Haskell -Wmissing-signatures)

A top-level binding without a sibling type signature has an inferred type that changes silently when its body does. Write the signature (Haskell -Wmissing-signatures).

```
Before:
  double x = x * 2
After:
  double : Int -> Int
  double x = x * 2
```

## rule-not-eq

negated equality `not (a == b)` / `not (a /= b)`. Prefer `a /= b` / `a == b`

A negated equality test has a direct operator.

```
Before:
  not (a == b)
After:
  a /= b
```

## rule-bool-simplify

redundant boolean shape (`if c then True else False`, `x == True`, `not (not x)`, …). Simplify

A boolean expression with a redundant shape: `if c then True else False`, `x == True`, `not (not x)`. Each simplifies to a shorter equivalent.

```
Before:
  if ok then True else False
After:
  ok
```

## rule-rem-parity

`n % 2 == 0` / `n % 2 /= 0` parity test. Prefer `isEven n` / `isOdd n`

A remainder-by-two comparison against zero is a parity test; the prelude names it.

```
Before:
  n % 2 == 0
After:
  isEven n
```

## rule-double-reverse

`reverse (reverse x)` is `x`. Drop the double reversal

Reversing a list twice returns the original list after two traversals.

```
Before:
  reverse (reverse xs)
After:
  xs
```

## rule-fuse-list-pipeline

a traversal with a single stdlib name: `somes (map f xs)`, `length (filter p xs)`, `length xs == 0`, `xs == []`

Several traversals build an intermediate list, or count a whole list to learn whether it is empty, where one stdlib name does the work in one pass.

```
Before:
  length (filter p xs)
  length xs == 0
  xs == []
After:
  count p xs
  isEmpty xs
  isEmpty xs
```

## rule-when-unless

`if b then m else pure ()` / `if b then pure () else m`. Prefer `when b m` / `unless b m`

An `if` with `pure ()` in one branch is `when` or `unless`.

```
Before:
  if b then act else pure ()
After:
  when b act
```

## rule-complement-predicate

`not (p x)` where `p` has a defined complement predicate (`isEmptyL`/`isSome`/`isOk` & inverses). Call the complement directly

Negating a predicate that has a defined complement (`isEmptyL`/`isSome`/`isOk` and their inverses) is clearer as a call to the complement.

```
Before:
  not (isSome x)
After:
  isNone x
```

## rule-match-to-map

2-arm `match` on Option/Result that reconstructs the failure ctor and re-wraps the success ctor. That IS a functor `map` (hlint 'use fmap')

A two-arm `match` on an `Option` or `Result` that passes the failure constructor through and re-wraps the success value is `map` (hlint "use fmap").

```
Before:
  match r
    Ok v => Ok (f v)
    Err e => Err e
After:
  map f r
```

## rule-option-eliminators

2-arm `match` on an Option/Result that unwraps with a literal, constructor or local-variable default, panics with a message, or answers whether it is `Some`. The prelude names these: `optionOr`, `optionOrPanic`, `isSome`, `isNone`, `resultOr`

A two-arm `match` that returns the payload of `Some`/`Ok` and otherwise a literal, a nullary constructor or a local variable is `optionOr`/`resultOr`; one that otherwise panics with a message is `optionOrPanic`; one that only answers `True`/`False` is `isSome`/`isNone`. A default that is a call or a top-level value is left alone: the function form evaluates it eagerly. The `optionOrPanic` fix needs `--unsafe-fixes`, because a native panic through it loses the call site's location.

```
Before:
  match o
    Some x => x
    None => 0
After:
  optionOr 0 o
```

## rule-eager-default

a call passed as the default of `optionOr`/`resultOr`, or as the argument of `whenL False`: it runs although its result is discarded. Use `optionOrElse`/`resultOrElse`

`optionOr d o` and `resultOr d r` are ordinary calls, so `d` is evaluated before the call even when `o` is `Some` or `r` is `Ok`. A default that is a call is wasted work on every hit, and an effect or a panic in it happens anyway. `optionOrElse` and `resultOrElse` take a function that runs on the miss only. A literal, a variable, a tuple, an operator expression or a constructor application is not reported, and neither is a partial application such as `map (optionOr d) xs`, which the lazy form would run once per miss.

`whenL False (f x)` is reported without a fix: its argument is evaluated although the guard is `False`.

```
Before:
  optionOr (freshVar ctx ()) (lookup n sub)
After:
  optionOrElse (_ => freshVar ctx ()) (lookup n sub)
```

## rule-bind-chain-to-do

deep (≥3) nested Result/Option passthrough-bind `match` pyramid. Rewrite as a `do` block (suggest-only)

Three or more nested `match` arms that each pass a `Result` or `Option` failure straight through form a pyramid. A `do` block flattens it. The rule only suggests; it has no fixer.

```
Before:
  match a
    Ok x => match b x
      Ok y => match c y
        Ok z => Ok z
        Err e => Err e
      Err e => Err e
    Err e => Err e
After:
  do
    x <- a
    y <- b x
    c y
```

## rule-dead-code

private (unexported) top-level binding is unreachable from the file's exports/main/doctests. Dead code (Haskell -Wunused-top-binds)

A private top-level binding that nothing reachable from the file's exports, `main` or doctests uses is dead code (Haskell -Wunused-top-binds). Delete it or export it.

```
Before:
  helper x = x + 1   -- never called
After:
  (binding removed)
```

## rule-unused-import

an imported name that nothing in the file uses

A name listed in `import m.{…}` that no expression, signature, constraint, pattern, doctest, `test` or `prop` body of the file uses is dead weight and hides which imports matter. `public import` re-exports, `import m.*`, bare `import m` and `import m as A` list no names and are not checked, and a `T(..)` member is never reported, since a constructor use is not tied to `T`. The fix drops the name and its comma; when no name of the line is used it leaves a bare `import m`, which still brings the module's `impl`s into scope.

```
Before:
  import list.{sort, nub}
  main = sort [2, 1]
After:
  import list.{sort}
  main = sort [2, 1]
```

## rule-unused-param

a function, method or `prop` parameter that nothing in its clause uses

A parameter that no use in its clause resolves to is dead weight, and a reader cannot tell it from one that matters. Renaming it `_name` says it is intentionally unused, and a name starting with `_` is not reported. Function, impl-method, interface-default, `prop`, `where` and top-level `let rec` clause parameters are checked; the parameters of a `let rec` written inside a block, and lambda, `let`, match-arm and `do`-bind binders, are not. The fix renames every place the binder is written (each alternative of an or-pattern names it). An unused as-binder `x@p` is not renamed: the fix drops `x@` and keeps the pattern. The rename is only suggested, not applied, when `_name` is already used in the declaration, and for a record pun, where renaming the binder would rename the field: the suggestion then reads `field = _name`.

```
Before:
  area w h = w * 2
After:
  area w _h = w * 2
```

## rule-unused-local

a `let` binder that nothing reads

A `let` binder that no use resolves to is either dead work or a missed use. Delete the binding if the bound expression has no effect, or use the name if it was meant to be read. A name starting with `_` is not reported; the intended discard is `let _ =` in `do` code and a bare statement elsewhere. Only plain and `do` `let` binders are checked; parameter, lambda, match-arm and `<-` bind binders are not. The finding is only suggested, never fixed, because the bound expression may run an effect.

```
Before:
  let total = sum xs
  count xs
After:
  count xs
```

## rule-concat-to-interp

`++` chain mixing string literals and expressions. Prefer string interpolation `"…\{e}…"` (hlint 'use interpolation')

A `++` chain mixing string literals with expressions reads better as string interpolation.

```
Before:
  "n = " ++ show n ++ "!"
After:
  "n = \{show n}!"
```

## rule-self-shadow-extern

top-level binding unconditionally forwards to itself (`f s = f s`, `x = x`) — an infinite self-recursion, not a forward to a same-named extern (#266)

A top-level binding that unconditionally forwards to itself (`f s = f s`, `x = x`) is an infinite recursion, usually an extern wrapper that forgot it shadows the extern it meant to call (#266).

```
Before:
  strLen s = strLen s
After:
  call the extern under its real name
```

## rule-prefer-assign-op

`setRef r v` (predates the `:=` write operator), or a `:=` write bound to a wildcard `let _ =`. Prefer `r := v` as a statement

`setRef r v` predates the `:=` write operator, and a `:=` write bound to a wildcard `let _ =` is a statement in disguise.

```
Before:
  setRef counter 1
After:
  counter := 1
```

## rule-let-underscore-unit

`let _ = e` on a call that returns Unit, in a plain block. Write the bare statement `e`

A call whose declared result is Unit has no value to bind, so `let _ =` in front of it says nothing. In a plain block the call is a statement on its own; `do` blocks keep `let _ =`. Only a saturated call to a signed function is checked: the declared result decides, so a partial application, a method, a shadowed name and an unsigned function are not reported.

```
Before:
  let _ = writeLine out "done"
  count xs
After:
  writeLine out "done"
  count xs
```

## rule-discarded-result

`let _ = e` on a call that returns a Result or an Option, in a plain block. Propagate it, handle it or name the discard

A call whose declared result is a `Result` or an `Option` carries a failure or an absence, and `let _ =` throws it away unread. In a plain block the error must be propagated (the enclosing function's type permits `?`, a match or `andThen`, or its signature changes with its callers), or the discard named with `bestEffort "<reason>"`, whose reason says why this error is ignorable. A discarded `Option` has a `None` case to handle, or the call is rewritten so the result is not discarded. `do` blocks are not checked. Only a saturated call to a signed function is checked: the declared result decides, so a partial application, a method, a shadowed name and an unsigned function are not reported.

```
Before:
  let _ = writeFile path text
  next ()
After:
  bestEffort "the scratch file is advisory" (writeFile path text)
  next ()
```

## rule-promissory-reader

comment claims a symbol has no reader yet ("nothing reads this yet", "no reader yet", "do not add a reader") but the file reads it (#2550)

A comment claiming a symbol has no reader yet ("nothing reads this yet", "no reader yet", "do not add a reader") while the file reads it is stale and misleads the next editor (#2550). This enforces the repository comment register.

```
Before:
  -- nothing reads this yet
  cache = ...   -- read two screens down
After:
  delete or correct the comment
```

## rule-orelse-staircase

first-match probe staircase (≥2 nested `None`/`Err` fallthrough re-probes, each success arm handing its payload straight back). Where the probes are pure and cheap, rewrite with the lazy `orElseWith` / `findMap` (suggest-only)

Two or more nested `None`/`Err` fall-through re-probes, each success arm handing its payload straight back, are a first-match search. Suggest-only.

`orElse a b` takes VALUES, so every probe runs. Use the lazy forms for each probe after the first: `orElseWith a (_ => probe)` for `Option`, `optionOrElse (_ => probe) opt`, `resultOrElse (err => probe) res` for `Result`, or `findMap` when the probes are one function over a list.

No rewrite applies when a later probe is expensive, effectful, or the enclosing function's own recursion; a staircase whose later probe calls the enclosing function is not reported.

```
Before:
  match probeA x
    Some v => Some v
    None => match probeB x
      Some v => Some v
      None => probeC x
After:
  orElseWith (probeA x) (_ => orElseWith (probeB x) (_ => probeC x))
```

## rule-clone-type

two-constructor `data` with `Option`'s or `Result`'s constructor arities and no `impl` in the declaring file. Prefer the stdlib type (suggest-only)

A two-constructor `data` with the arities of `Option` or `Result` and no `impl` in its file duplicates the stdlib type and loses its instances. Suggest-only.

```
Before:
  data Maybe2 a = Nope | Yep a
After:
  use `Option a`
```

## rule-clause-map

two-clause `[]`/`(x :: xs)` recursion that conses a per-element transform onto the recursive call — a hand-written `map` (suggest-only)

A two-clause `[]` / `(x :: xs)` recursion that conses a per-element transform onto the recursive call is a hand-written `map`. Suggest-only.

```
Before:
  go [] = []
  go (x :: xs) = f x :: go xs
After:
  map f
```

## rule-duplicate-body

top-level function body is structurally identical to another top-level function in the SAME file (copy-paste; consolidate) — the in-file counterpart of the cross-file rule of the same name

Two top-level functions in the same file with structurally identical bodies (location-stripped, above a complexity floor) are copy-paste. Consolidate them. The cross-file arm of the same rule compares across files.

```
Before:
  f x = big x
  g y = big y   -- same body shape
After:
  one function, called twice
```

## rule-directive-reason

a `-- lint-disable-*` directive with no comment in its own comment block stating the constraint that forced it — an issue number alone is not a reason (#2862)

A `-- lint-disable-*` directive needs a comment in its own comment block stating the constraint that forced it; an issue number alone is not a reason (#2862). This enforces the repository suppression convention.

```
Before:
  -- lint-disable-next-line rule-x
After:
  -- bounded: at most 3 fields, so a list lookup is cheaper
  -- lint-disable-next-line rule-x
```

## rule-regex-literal

a string literal passed directly to `compile`/`mustCompile` fails to compile as a regex pattern

A string literal passed directly to `compile` or `mustCompile` that is not a valid regex fails at run time on every call. The rule compiles it at lint time.

```
Before:
  mustCompile "(unclosed"
After:
  mustCompile "(closed)"
```

## rule-test-bool-literal-equal

`expectEqual` against a `True`/`False` literal (either side). Prefer `expectTrue e` / `expectFalse e`

`expectEqual` against a `True`/`False` literal loses the operand in the failure message; use `expectTrue`/`expectFalse`. `--fix` rewrites it only where every verb involved is `test`'s own import: a verb that resolves to a local or top-level binding, or to another module's import, is left alone.

```
Before:
  expectEqual True (a == 1)
After:
  expectTrue (a == 1)
```

## rule-test-bool-helper

a `-> Bool` helper in a `*_test.mdk` whose call is graded with `expectTrue`/`expectFalse`. Return an `Expect` (`expectErrContains`, `expectEqual`, ...) so a failure says what was expected

A `Bool` helper graded with `expectTrue`/`expectFalse` fails with "expected True, got False" and names nothing. Make the helper return an `Expect` built from the verb that fits (`expectErrContains`, `expectEqual`, `expectOk`, ...; see the `write-tests` table) and drop the `expectTrue`/`expectFalse` wrapper at its call sites. A helper that a `prop` in the same file references keeps `Bool`, because a prop's oracle is `Bool`. Covered call shapes: `expectTrue (h a b)`, `expectFalse (h a b)`, `h a b |> expectTrue`, `x |> h |> expectTrue`. Not covered: a call nested deeper in the argument (`expectTrue (a && h b)`, `expectTrue (not (h b))`).

```
Before:
  rejects : String -> Bool
  test "t" = expectTrue (rejects "x")
After:
  rejects : String -> Expect
  test "t" = rejects "x"
```

## rule-test-equal-in-true

an `==`/`/=` comparison wrapped in `expectTrue`/`expectFalse`. Prefer `expectEqual a b` / `expectNotEqual a b`, which report both operands on failure

An `==`/`/=` comparison wrapped in `expectTrue`/`expectFalse` reports neither operand on failure; use `expectEqual`/`expectNotEqual`. `--fix` rewrites it only where every verb involved is `test`'s own import: a verb that resolves to a local or top-level binding, or to another module's import, is left alone.

```
Before:
  expectTrue (a == b)
After:
  expectEqual a b
```

## rule-prelude-shadow

a module declares a top-level `isOk`/`isErr`/`isSome`/`isNone`, shadowing the prelude function of that name (suggest-only)

A module that declares a top-level `isOk`, `isErr`, `isSome` or `isNone` shadows the prelude function of that name for the rest of the file, while every other module keeps calling the prelude one. A module that declares the `Option` or `Result` type itself, as the prelude does, is not shadowing the names over that type. Suggest-only. Delete the local copy when it behaves like the prelude one; otherwise rename it to say what it tests.

```
Before:
  isSome o = o == 1
After:
  isOne o = o == 1
```

## rule-accumulator-append

`acc ++ e` grown across a loop: each step copies the whole accumulator. Cons then `reverse`, collect then join once, or use a builder

Appending to the end of an accumulator copies the accumulator, so a loop that does it once per step does work quadratic in the length of the result. The rule reports three shapes: a self-call that passes `acc ++ e` for one of its own parameters, `r := !r ++ e` on a `Ref` inside a self-recursive function, and a fold lambda `acc x => acc ++ ...`. The same holds for a `List`, a `String` and a `Bytes`. `e ++ acc` is not reported: for a `List` it costs only the length of `e`, while a `String`, `Bytes` or `Array` copies both operands. A partial application and a call to a different function (mutual recursion) are not self-calls.

Cons the new element and `reverse` once at the end, collect the pieces and join them once (`concat`, `joinWith`), or use a builder. A loop whose bound is small and fixed can carry a `-- lint-disable-next-line rule-accumulator-append` with the bound as its reason.

```
Before:
  go acc (x :: xs) = go (acc ++ [f x]) xs
After:
  go acc (x :: xs) = go (f x :: acc) xs  -- and `reverse acc` at the end
```

## rule-reslice-in-loop

a loop parameter re-sliced from its start on every step: quadratic on some engines and access patterns. Walk a `StrCursor`, or convert with `toChars` once

A self-recursive loop that passes a `String`, `Array` or `Bytes` parameter on unchanged while another argument advances, and slices that parameter by the advancing index, starts from the front of the parameter on every step. The rule reports the String externs `stringSlice` and `charAtStr` on such a parameter, and `slice`, `sliceClamped`, `drop` and `a.[lo..hi]` on a parameter whose declared type, in the enclosing top-level signature, is `String`, `Array` or `Bytes`. A `List` parameter is skipped (`drop` on a list is the loop itself), and so is a slice whose bounds mention no advancing name. A partial application and a call to a different function (mutual recursion) are not self-calls. `stringSliceBytes` is not reported: it copies only the piece and does not walk the string.

For a `String`, `stringSlice` and `charAtStr` locate their offset from the front of the string. On the native runtime a forward scan of one string is linear, because the runtime keeps a cursor cache for one string; the loop is quadratic when it alternates between two strings, goes backward or slices the tail, and on the WasmGC engine, which has no cache, even a forward scan is quadratic. Walk a `StrCursor` (`startCursor`, `nextChar`, `sliceBetween`), or convert once with `toChars` and index the `Array`. A loop whose bound is small and fixed can carry a `-- lint-disable-next-line rule-reslice-in-loop` with the bound as its reason.

```
Before:
  go s i = if i < stringLength s then stringSlice i (i + 1) s :: go s (i + 1) else []
After:
  go cs i = if i < length cs then cs.[i] :: go cs (i + 1) else []  -- with `cs = toChars s`
```

## rule-list-as-set

a `List` a loop grows and membership-tests on every step: each test walks the whole list. Keep a `Set` or `Map` beside it, or build the set once

A membership test on a `List` (`contains`, `elem`, `notElem`, `lookupAssoc`, `lookup`, or a hand-rolled function of the file that walks a list and returns `Bool` or `Option`) walks the list. When a loop grows the list and tests it on every step, the loop does work quadratic in the number of steps. The rule reports a membership test whose container is a parameter that a self-call of the same function passes grown (`x :: seen`, `seen ++ xs`, `xs ++ seen`, a `let` bound to one of those, or a helper of the file that returns its argument grown), and a test on the accumulator of a fold lambda that returns the accumulator grown. A test made by a helper of the same file that the loop calls with the list is reported at the call. A container that is only passed on unchanged or shrinks is not reported, nor is one held in a `Ref`, a record field or a top-level table, nor a test two helpers away. A partial application and a call to a different function (mutual recursion) are not self-calls. `*_test.mdk` files are not checked.

Keep the names in a `Set` (or the pairs in a `Map`) beside the list, or build the set once before the loop. A list whose length is small and fixed can carry a `-- lint-disable-next-line rule-list-as-set` with the bound as its reason.

```
Before:
  go seen (x :: xs) = if contains x seen then go seen xs else go (x :: seen) xs
After:
  go seen (x :: xs) = if has x seen then go seen xs else go (insert x seen) xs  -- with `seen : Set String`
```

## rule-walker-wildcard

a self-recursive function over constructor patterns ends in a wildcard that returns a constant or its input without recursing: a new constructor is silently skipped

A function that calls itself, has at least two clauses or match arms on constructors of one sum, and ends in a wildcard whose body is a literal, a constant constructor or its input unchanged, treats every constructor it does not name as a leaf. When the sum later gains a constructor, nothing goes red: the walker skips its subtree. The rule names the constructors the wildcard swallows, found in the file's own `data` declarations or the project index; when the sum cannot be resolved it says so and reports an unknown count.

Name the swallowed constructors in an or-pattern, so adding one is a visible edit, or recurse into them. A wildcard that is a deliberate default for three or more constructors takes a `-- lint-disable-next-line rule-walker-wildcard` that says why. Recursion counts only in a clause whose body also uses a field its constructor pattern binds. A wildcard that swallows only constructors without fields hides no subtree and is not reported. A wildcard that recurses, a function with fewer than two constructor clauses, and a function that is not self-recursive are not reported.

```
Before:
  usesVar x (EVar y) = x == y
  usesVar x (EApp f a) = usesVar x f || usesVar x a
  usesVar _ _ = False
After:
  usesVar x (EVar y) = x == y
  usesVar x (EApp f a) = usesVar x f || usesVar x a
  usesVar x (ELam _ body) = usesVar x body
  usesVar _ (ELit _ | EListLit _) = False
```

## rule-threaded-invariant

a self-recursive function passes two or more of its parameters through every self-call unchanged: close over them in a where-local `go`

A top-level function that calls itself with the same two or more parameters, in the same positions, in every self-call carries those parameters through the whole recursion for nothing. A local `go` in a `where` closes over them, so the recursion names only what changes. The rule reads each function as a group of clauses: a position counts when every full-arity self-call of every clause that makes one passes that clause's own parameter there, unchanged. One invariant parameter is not reported, nor is a `go` that already closes over its invariants, a partial application, mutual recursion, or a loop local to a `let` or `where`.

`--fix --unsafe-fixes` writes the `go` form when the whole shape is known: a signature whose class constraints the closed-over parameters carry, each invariant parameter a plain name (or ignored) in every clause, no list builder in tail position modulo cons, no invariant parameter used only to be passed on, and a `where` of its own only on a single clause. The rest are reported only. Run `medaka fmt --write` after it, then check the converted loop for dictionary dispatch: `go` is inferred, not declared, so a changing parameter whose type only the signature fixes (a counter under `+` or `==`, an element that is interpolated) is let-generalised and the loop passes a dictionary on every call (#4921, MonoLocalBinds). The fix does not see that shape.

```
Before:
  extractFold bare heads acc (x :: xs) = extractFold bare heads (step bare heads acc x) xs
  extractFold _ _ acc [] = acc
After:
  extractFold bare heads acc0 xs0 = go acc0 xs0
    where
      go acc [] = acc
      go acc (x :: xs) = go (step bare heads acc x) xs
```

## rule-passthrough-arm

a two-arm `match` over an Option/Result with a verbatim `None => None` / `Err e => Err e` arm: bind in a `do` block instead

A `match` that passes a failure straight through (`None => None`, or `Err e => Err e` with the same variable) and continues in the other arm is a monadic bind written by hand. Write it as a `do` block, at any depth: one level is enough, unlike `rule-bind-chain-to-do`, which needs a pyramid of three. `--fix --unsafe-fixes` rewrites the statement-position cases; the rest are reported only.

Not reported: a failure arm that rebuilds its value (`Err e => Err (wrap e)`), a match with a third arm or a guard, a success arm that re-wraps in the same constructor (`rule-match-to-map` owns it). A match whose success arm ends, through `if`, `let`, `match` arms and block tails, in a call of the enclosing function (a self-recursive tail, including a where-local `go`) is not reported: the `do` form lowers to `andThen`, which allocates a closure per iteration and measurably slows the loop.

```
Before:
  match catalogRow n
    Some r => g r
    None => None
After:
  do
    r <- catalogRow n
    g r
```

## rule-comment-history

comment line narrates history ("formerly", "used to", "The old ", "Until 2026-")

A comment line that narrates what the code used to be ("formerly", "used to", "withdrawn", "The old ", "Until 2026-") goes stale the day it is written; state the constraint the code carries now.

```
Before:
  -- formerly a list, now a map
After:
  -- keyed by name so lookups stay O(log n)
```

## rule-comment-ruling

comment line uses reviewer-addressed ruling vocabulary ("refuted", "ratified", "withdrawn")

Ruling vocabulary ("refuted", "ratified", "withdrawn", "ruling") addresses a reviewer; it belongs on the PR or issue, not in the source.

```
Before:
  -- ratified in review
After:
  -- the invariant the review settled, stated directly
```

## rule-comment-tombstone

comment line is a tombstone for code that no longer exists

A tombstone ("was HERE and is RETIRED", "do not re-add", "now lives in", "moved to", "now comes from") points at code that is gone.

```
Before:
  -- moved to util.mdk
After:
  delete the comment
```

## rule-comment-emoji

comment line carries an emoji shout

An emoji shout (a siren, a warning sign or a lock) in a comment; state the constraint in words.

```
Before:
  -- (siren) never edit this
After:
  -- byte-pinned by a gate: edits break its golden
```

## rule-comment-draft

comment line narrates a draft ("earlier cut", "first cut", "earlier revision")

Draft self-narration ("earlier cut", "first cut", "earlier revision") describes the author's process, not the code.

```
Before:
  -- the first cut used a list
After:
  delete the comment
```

## rule-comment-deictic

comment line points at "this PR"

A comment that says "this PR" does not survive the PR merging.

```
Before:
  -- added in this PR
After:
  delete the comment
```

## rule-comment-dead-path

comment line cites a dead OCaml path (lib/*.ml)

A comment that cites a path under lib/ ending in .ml points at the removed OCaml compiler.

```
Before:
  -- see lib/typecheck.ml
After:
  cite the Medaka module that holds the code
```

## rule-comment-shout

comment line has three consecutive capitalised words

Three consecutive words in capitals read as shouting; state the constraint in plain words.

```
Before:
  -- (caps) do not edit this
After:
  -- byte-pinned by a gate
```

## rule-comment-provenance-id

comment line carries a plan sub-id ("#2400 F3", "#1111 A-2.3")

A plan sub-id after an issue number ("#2400 F3", "#838 I1", "#1111 A-2.3") records which work item introduced the code; state the constraint the code carries now. A pointer to an issue the code waits on stays.

```
Before:
  -- #2400 F3: unlocated diagnostics keep the placeholder
After:
  -- unlocated diagnostics keep the placeholder
```

## rule-comment-stale-backtick

a backticked identifier in a comment names nothing the project or the stdlib declares, and occurs in no code line of the file (#4319)

A comment that names a function or value in backticks goes stale when the name is renamed or deleted, and no other gate notices. The rule reads each backticked lowercase identifier in a prose comment and accepts it when it is a declaration in the project or stdlib index, a record field or a module-name segment there, a Medaka keyword, or a whole word on some code line of the same file. A name spelled like no Medaka declaration is skipped: three characters or fewer, a mangled `__` name, a C-runtime, C-library or gate-name prefix, a hex hash, or a word of SQL, LLVM IR, WebAssembly, C or the shell. Anything else names a thing that is gone, or a local of another file: point the comment at the live top-level name, restate the constraint without it, or delete the comment.

```
Before:
  -- see `oldHelper` for the cache key
After:
  -- see `cacheKey` for the cache key
```
